20186-the-dismal-swamp-and-lake-drummond:
The Dismal Swamp and Lake Drummond recalls early efforts to use Virginia's great swamp. George Washington held land there through the Dismal Swamp Land Company. After the Revolutionary War, that company set hands to cutting timber. A large amount of timber was cut and readied for sale.

Yet the timber needed an outlet that swamp roads could not give. Only a canal or ditch could float it out to buyers. Washington thus backed ditch and canal work in the swamp's heart. Readers get local history mixed with vivid, amusing scenes from swamp life.
20512-man-and-maid:
Elinor Glyn's novel Man and Maid opens in the voice of a soldier broken by the Great War. He looks at his mutilated face before he puts the black patch over his left eye. His shoulder is crooked, and his right leg is gone from the knee down.

With such a wreck of a man, he believes, no woman can feel emotion for him again in this world. The novel tests that despair against love. Glyn, famous for romantic fiction, writes here about wounds that show and wounds that hide, in the hard years just after the war.
20678-the-tory-maid:
Herbert Baird's The Tory Maid, published in 1898, is a romance of the American Revolution in Maryland. The narrator writes as an old man, looking back on the wild days of his youth. He settles on the great porch of Fairlee to tell his story, with old friends around him.

With a julep on his right hand and the paper before him, he takes up the pen. He writes of the days when he first drew his sword in the Great Cause. The maid of the title holds Tory loyalties, and love across the divide drives the tale Baird builds.
21275-the-goat-and-her-kid:
Mrs Harriet Myrtle's stories for young children were issued in New York in 1870 in the Rose-Bud Stories series. They open on a bright green grass plot behind a cottage. A goat nibbles there all day with her pretty kid running at her side. But this kid loves dancing and frisking more than any kid in the village.

A poor Italian boy comes down the lane playing a pipe and tabor for two dancing dolls, and the kid's adventures begin. Other tales in the little book include one on young birds tumbling from the nest and a final piece, Winter Pleasures. Myrtle wrote simply, for the youngest readers.
22047-the-love-affairs-of-an-old-maid:
Lilian Bell published The Love Affairs of an Old Maid in 1893 under a teasing title. Her narrator is a spinster who reviews, with dry honesty, the loves of her life. She admits she dares to be brutally frank only with herself. To the world she keeps a proper face, but on paper nothing is spared.

Each affair is recalled in turn, with its hopes, blunders, and quiet endings. Bell writes bright, chatty comedy rather than tragedy. The book plays with the idea that an "old maid" may have had more romance than her married friends. It was light reading with a sharp edge, popular in the 1890s.
22538-the-devil-s-asteroid:
Manly Wade Wellman wrote The Devil's Asteroid, a science fiction adventure of space exile. A skipper with a rolling accent lands his ship under orders. Prisoners get thirty seconds, Earth time, to clear the blast.

Now we ground, the skipper announces as the shock comes. The inner panel opens, then the outer hatch, into beating sunlight. Goodbye, he says formally to the man put ashore alone. Thirty seconds to walk clear before the ship takes off again. That cruel farewell launches the stranded man's fight to survive. An asteroid that works as a prison gives the tale its title. Readers get pulp space adventure with a lone convict's odds.
23045-measure-for-measure-the-works-of-w:
The Duke hands over Vienna in Measure for Measure, printed here from the Cambridge Shakespeare. The Duke declines to lecture Angelo on ruling. Angelo's own knowledge of government, he says, passes any counsel he could offer. Nothing remains but to let that competence do its work.

What Angelo does with that power drives Shakespeare's darkest comedy. Puritan strictness meets its own appetites, and the disguised Duke watches his city from the shadows. The Cambridge editors' notes track the text's early printings in their usual detail. Of all the plays here, this one argues hardest with its audience. Justice, mercy, and desire each get measured, and none comes out exact.
428-frivolous-cupid:
Anthony Hope, writing as Sir Anthony Hope Hawkins, gathers eight light tales of love and marriage in this volume. Young men home from school, lawn-tennis clubs, and country houses set the scenes. Suitors dither, change heart, repent, and marry by compulsion, all under Cupid's teasing rule.

The opening tale follows Harry Sterling, back from Harrow and bound for Oxford, as old playmates greet him as a new man. Later stories weigh why men shun marriage and how a firm heart may still win. Hope writes with wit and ease, and the book reads as a graceful comedy of courtship.
440-just-david:
Eleanor Porter tells of David, a boy raised alone with his father in a mountain shack, in this gentle novel. David knows music, nature, and his father's violin, but little of town ways. When his father dies, David must come down to the valley and learn its puzzling dos and don'ts among strangers.

Porter follows David through discords, nuisances, and small rescues, as his music softens hard hearts. A lady of roses, a tower window, and a castle in Spain fill his dreams. The book charms as a warm tale of innocence meeting the world, and of beauty found in plain things.
457-the-price-she-paid:
David Graham Phillips opens this novel with the death of Henry Gower, a man praised as generous yet selfish to the core. His widow and children, kept in luxury for his own comfort, find he saved nothing for them. His daughter must now face the world with beauty, pride, and little cash.

Phillips follows her through suitors, stages, and bargains as she learns what each choice costs. The price of the title is paid in pride, love, and years. The novel reads as a sharp study of a family built on a fraud, and of a woman who must earn her own worth.
784-boyhood-in-norway-stories-of-boy-lif:
Hjalmar Hjorth Boyesen wrote these stories of boy life in Norway, the land of the midnight sun. Tales such as The Battle of the Rafts, The Clash of Arms, and Biceps Grimlund's Christmas Vacation follow lads at school, on farms, and by fjords. Snow, boats, and hard play shape their days.

Boyesen, himself Norwegian-born, writes with warmth for the old country and its customs, from Christmas feasts to tales of Vikings retold by boys. The stories praise pluck, fair play, and loyalty, without hiding the cold or the risk. The book gives young readers a vivid, affectionate tour of Norway as it was.
an-old-maid:
Honoré de Balzac sets his novel in Alençon, a quiet French town, where the rich and aging Mademoiselle Cormon wishes at last to marry. Her choice of husband becomes the town's great contest. Katharine Prescott Wormeley translated the book, as its title page states. Two rivals scheme for her hand and her fortune.

Seven chapters follow the Chevalier de Valois, the scheming du Bousquier, and the gentle young Athanase, who loves her in silence. Balzac mixes comedy about provincial manners with a sadder look at pride, gossip, and wasted hope. The ending, named in the contents as a final disappointment, lands with real sting.
boyhood-in-norway-stories-of-boy-life-in:
Hjalmar Hjorth Boyesen, a Norwegian immigrant who became an American professor, wrote Boyhood in Norway as linked stories of boy life in the land of the midnight sun. The Battle of the Rafts opens the book with a deadly feud between East-Side and West-Side boys in Numedale. Rafts, ambushes, and thrashings follow the rules of boy warfare.

Other tales give Biceps Grimlund's Christmas vacation, a masquerade, the story of a horse, and Bonnyboy, plus a bear that had a bank account. Boyesen writes from his own Norwegian childhood, keeping the scenery, school customs, and sagas in the background. The stories balance mischief with moral consequence, and preserve a rural Norway of the 1850s.
by-england-s-aid: By England's Aid, G. A. Henty's tale of the Netherlands. The English aid. This book preserves that historical novel. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-armand-david:
Armand David, missionary priest and zoologist, was born in 1826 and died in 1900. He joined the Congregation of the Mission in 1848, already fond of the natural sciences, and was ordained in 1862. Soon sent to Peking, he began a natural history collection, mainly zoological, with botany, geology, and palaeontology well represented. At the French government's request, important specimens went to Paris and stirred great interest.

The Jardin des Plantes then commissioned him to make scientific journeys through China for further collections. He obtained many specimens of animals and plants hitherto unknown. His collections won wide recognition for advancing systematic zoology, the classification of animals, and above all animal geography, the study of where species live. He summed up his labours to the International Scientific Congress of Catholics in Paris.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernard-john-:
Bernard John McQuaid, first bishop of Rochester in New York, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born in New York City in 1823 to an Irish father from Tyrone, he died at Rochester in 1909. Mass was first said in his family's Jersey City home in 1829, and he trained at Chambly in Quebec and St. John's Seminary at Fordham.

Ordained in 1848, he served in New Jersey and New York parishes before Rochester made him its first bishop. There he built parishes across the diocese, organized a parochial school system within ten years, and opened St. Andrew's and St. Bernard's seminaries. The entry presents a founder-bishop who shaped a diocese from its first day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christoph-von:
An entry on Christoph von Schmid, a writer of children's stories and educator born in Bavaria in August 1768. He studied theology at Dillingen, was ordained in 1791, and served in parishes until 1796, when he took charge of a school at Thannhausen on the Mindel. There he began writing for children, starting with First Lessons about God for the Little Ones, then a Bible History for Children.

Schmid wrote not for an unknown public or for money, but for the children around him. He read stories after school as a reward and asked them to write the tales down at home. In this way he learned how children think and speak, and he kept to their language rather than bookish speech. From 1816 to 1826 he served as Oberstadion's parish priest, then canon of Augsburg. His stories, translated into twenty-four languages, still rank him first among Germany's children's writers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-el-cid:
El Cid, Rodrigo Diaz, Count of Bivar, was the great popular hero of chivalrous Spain, born at Burgos about 1040 and dead at Valencia in 1099. The Moors called him seid, or cid, meaning lord, and his own people called him campeador, meaning champion. Tradition has wrapped him in legend so thickly that even his existence has been doubted, though the entry finds no good reason to doubt it.

History and romance give two different men. History shows a freebooting adventurer who fought Christians and Moors alike and plundered for his own gain, though much of that picture comes from hostile Arab writers. Romance shows a tender husband and father, a generous conqueror, and a loyal servant of king and country. The entry asks readers to judge him by the standards of his own age, not ours, and traces the wars of Ferdinand I's sons that framed his career.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gheeraert-dav:
Gheeraert David was a Flemish painter born at Oudewater around 1450, who died at Bruges on 13 August 1523. He entered the Guild of Saint Luke there as a master painter in 1484 and became its dean in 1501. His early training is unknown, though his work shows Florentine and Venetian touches. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows his life from wandering assistant to settled Bruges master.

In 1496 he married Cornelia Cnoop, and they had one daughter, Barbara. He gathered the best traditions of his predecessors rather than striking a new path, and his saints look more sedate than those of Memling. He created a lasting type of the Child Jesus, painted strong portraits, and excelled in brocades, embroidery, and landscape. His Virgo inter Virgines, given in 1509 to the Carmelite nuns of Sion at Bruges, ranks among his finest works. His paintings hang in London, Dublin, Bruges, Rouen, Sigmaringen, and Vienna.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-herenaus-haid:
Herenaus Haid, a catechist born in the diocese of Ratisbon in 1784, grew up destitute and worked as a shepherd's boy. He learned from his mother only the rosary and the catechism of Canisius. Despite privation he finished studies at Neuburg and theology at Landshut, took his doctorate at Munich in 1808, and, through Sailer, taught exegesis at St. Gall from 1813 to 1818. Recalled to Munich, he was relegated to a country parish in 1824, but returned under Ludwig honoured by his bishop.

Haid's life work was the catechism course in his Munich church, described in his seven-volume work of 1837 to 1845. This sets out a theory of catechetics stressing the Roman catechism and Canisius's. His veneration for Canisius, held since boyhood, led him to edit and translate his works and write his biography. Afflicted with blindness in his closing years, he bore it with resignation until his death in 1873, near ninety.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-king-david: This 1913 reference article on David — the psalmist king. John Corbett unfolds his shepherd's tale. He slew the Philistine giant. Israel crowned the beloved name. The Psalms keep his memory. His 10th-century reign is famed. His psalms are famed. His 10th-century psalms are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-ceolfrid: St. Ceolfrid was the abbot of Wearmouth-Jarrow. This entry traces his Bede, his Codex Amiatinus, and his fame. The master of the Northumbrian scriptorium: his great Codex crowned Rome in the 716 of the journey from Jarrow in the north.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-david: St. David was the patron of Wales. This long entry examines his Menevia, his leeks, and his fame. The bishop of the Welsh church: his ancient see crowned Menevia in the 500s' Wales in the west of the principality in the diocese.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-diarmaid: St. Diarmaid was the abbot of the Irish house. This entry traces his monastery, his rule, and his cult. The founder of the midland abbey: his famed rule crowned the 500s in the abbey of the midlands in the county.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-wilfrid: St. Wilfrid was the bishop of York. This long entry examines his Whitby, his Rome, and his fame. The champion of the Roman party: his great see crowned York in the 660s' Northumbria in the Ouse of the river in England.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thebaid: The Thebaid was the desert of the monks. This long entry examines its Anthony, its cells, and its history. The wilderness of the Egyptian fathers: their lonely cells crowned the desert in the 300s of the Anthony in the wadi.

doe-osti-3365378-strategies-for-flood-re: Iowa's storms don't spare the power grid, and floods knock out the poles and wires that serve farms and towns. eve-and-david:
Honore de Balzac's Eve and David, translated by Ellen Marriage, forms the third part of Lost Illusions, as its preparer's note explains. Lucien has gone to Paris; his sister Eve and her husband David Sechard, the idealist printer of Angouleme, remain to face his debts and their enemies, the Cointet brothers. David's paper-making invention draws spies and lawsuits.

The Angouleme chapters alternate workshop, law court, and the forged bills that ruin the couple, while Eve offers the returning Lucien their last crust of bread. Balzac knew printing from his own failed business, and the technical detail is exact. The volume closes the trilogy's contrast between Parisian ambition and provincial loyalty.
frivolous-cupid:
Anthony Hope, writing as the Anthony Hope who created The Prisoner of Zenda, gathered eight light love stories in Frivolous Cupid. Titles like Why Men Don't Marry, A Change of Heart, and Marriage By Compulsion announce the tone. The first tale returns Harry Sterling to the lawn-tennis club at Natterley, where little happens and everything is noticed.

Suitors hesitate, girls maneuver, curates and cousins complicate engagements, and Cupid behaves frivolously throughout. Hope's dialogue is quick and his plotting neat, with each story turning on a small misunderstanding or a change of mind. Readers wanting Edwardian romantic comedy, polished and brief, will find these tales easy company.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FaginDavid_Fagi:
Harold Weisberg wrote to David Fagin in April 1975 with advice Fagin had not asked for. The letter warns him about political dabbling, the world of campaigns and causes where a young man could be used. Weisberg, who watched that world closely, offered the benefit of his suspicion.

Along the way the letter criticizes Mark Lane, the best-known early critic of the Warren Report, and discusses Wesley Liebeler, a former commission lawyer. Weisberg's feuds and judgments fill the page. The letter shows the research community's rivalries as plainly as its research.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-KromanDavid_Kro:
The New York Times carried this United Press International report on March 28, 1967, from Bismarck, North Dakota. A judge had declared a mistrial in a Midwest insurance fraud case involving 53 million dollars. The ruling came after a lawyer in the case said he had been forced off a highway at gunpoint.

The lawyer said he was carrying documents when it happened. Those documents, he claimed, proved that President Kennedy was killed by people other than Lee Harvey Oswald. The wire story is brief. Still, it captures a strange moment when a fraud trial in North Dakota collided with the national argument over the assassination.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ObstDavid_Obst_: An unidentified reviewer took up a book by Martin Mayer about banking. The review says the book introduces the mysteries of banking, money, and the Federal Reserve to general readers. Mayer wrote widely read explanations of American institutions. The file does not name the publication or the reviewer, and it does not preserve the review's verdict, so only its subject and its approach can honestly be described.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-OsterlandDavid_:
An advertisement offers a 90-minute documentary with a long title: 'Kennedy Assassination: What Do We Know Now That We Didn't Know Then?' The film was assembled from government documents obtained under the Freedom of Information Act. It was sold to Panorama, the BBC's flagship current-affairs program.

A documentary built from FOIA paper was a new kind of product when this ad ran. The selling point was not a narrator's theory but the documents themselves, photographed and read on screen. The sale to the BBC shows the market: British television buying American paper to revisit Dallas. The advertisement preserves the pitch, the running time, and the buyer.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-SaulsburyDavid_:
Harold Weisberg wrote to David Saulsbury on August 29, 1993. He discusses Harrison Edward Livingstone's book 'Killing the Truth,' a rival's account he disputed. He complains of the Baltimore police's failure to act on a matter he brought them. He also writes about dangers he himself faced. The letter is late Weisberg: combative, specific, and still working.

By 1993, Weisberg was in his eighties and his letters still ran on three tracks at once: feuds with other researchers, fights with officials, and personal risk. The letter to Saulsbury holds all three. It preserves his voice at the end of a long campaign, and the names of the men and offices he was still arguing with.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ScheimDavid_Sch: nsia-ScheimDavid Scheim David: the made public government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item, complete, filed. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WroneDavidRBibl: David R. Wrone drafted a twelve-page prologue on journalism after Watergate. It criticizes the press for trusting anonymous sources and hidden informants once Nixon fell. Wrone, a historian of the Kennedy assassination, knew the leak-driven story well. The draft argues that nameless sourcing weakened reporting itself. Kept as a draft, it shows a scholar working out a charge against the press of his own time.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-:
In 1963 President John F. Kennedy fought a polite, relentless battle by letter with Israel's leaders over the Dimona reactor. William Burr and Avner Cohen edited this briefing book, number 671, published in May 2019. Kennedy's correspondents were David Ben-Gurion and then Levi Eshkol.

Kennedy warned that American commitment and support for Israel could be seriously jeopardized without inspection of Dimona. Intelligence estimated the reactor could soon produce enough plutonium for one or two weapons a year. The letters are diplomacy at its most personal: a president pressing an ally in writing, and an ally stalling in writing, with a bomb program between the lines.
just-david:
Just David is a novel by Eleanor H. Porter, author of Pollyanna. Its twenty-five chapters run from The Mountain Home to The Beautiful World. David lives with his father in a little shack far up a mountain-side. Cliffs break the north wind behind it, and a green slope falls away in front.

The contents promise a trail down to the valley, two letters, and a string of discords. David puzzles over the dos and don'ts of the world below. Jack and Jill, the Lady of the Roses, and David's castle in Spain fill the middle chapters. Porter's title calls him just David: a boy whose music and honesty work on every household he enters.
madge-morton-captain-of-the-merry-maid:
Madge Morton, Captain of the Merry Maid is a girls' adventure by Amy D. V. Chalmers. Henry Altemus published it at Philadelphia in 1914. Madge had already starred in three earlier books of the series. Here her houseboat vacation begins with a plan and a chaperon hunt.

The girls find their boat, name her the Merry Maid, and go aboard. Pleasure Bay, a girl on an island, and an anxious night follow. A storm puts them at the mercy of the waves. Rescue attempts and a capture raise the stakes for Mollie. Madge leads her crew with pluck through every scrape. It is wholesome, lively fun for young readers.
nasa-tm-19660030619-potentiometric-inves:
V. V. Lyul'ko first published this chemistry study in Russian in 1962, in the journal Khimiya i Khimicheskaya Tekhnologiya. Walter Urusky translated it into English, and the translation was issued on August 15, 1966, at Redstone Arsenal, Alabama. The work tracks, through voltage measurements, how oxygen slowly turns ferrous chloride into its oxidized form.

Lyul'ko notes that the reaction runs very slowly at room temperature, so speeding it up matters in practice. One use is removing iron impurities from zinc concentrates when producing non-ferrous metals. The paper examines how different catalyzers change the reaction rate. It also tests how hydrochloric acid levels and iron chloride levels affect the oxidation of bivalent iron ions at room temperature.
nasa-tm-19680010362-exploring-in-aerospa: Joseph F. McBride, at the Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, taught this lesson to the Lewis Aerospace Explorers in 1966 and 1967. It is chapter six of the series Exploring in Aerospace Rocketry, and its subject is solid-propellant rocket systems. The catalog record lists rocket design and how solid propellants burn, including how fast and how well. The hosted sample preserves only the cover and series list, with no readable body text.
the-imaginary-invalid:
Molière's Le Malade Imaginaire appears here in English prose. Charles Heron Wall translated it. Short introductions and notes come with his version. The headnote records poignant facts. This was the last comedy Molière wrote. He was very ill as he wrote it. He was nearly dying. The first performance came on February 10, 1673. The Palais Royal Theatre staged it. Molière himself acted the part of Argan.

The cast list lays out the farce. Argan is the imaginary invalid. Béline is his second wife. Angélique, his daughter, loves Cléante. Béralde is his sensible brother. Toinette serves as the maid. His doctor is Mr. Purgon. An apothecary attends him too. Dr. Diafoirus hopes his son Thomas will marry Angélique. That match is the medical marriage Argan wants. A hypochondriac among doctors gives Molière his target.
the-man-who-was-afraid:
Maxim Gorky's novel Foma Gordyeff was published in English as The Man Who Was Afraid, translated by Herman Bernstein. An introductory note hails Gorky in extravagant terms. Out of life's darkest depths, it says, comes the Byron of the twentieth century. He is the poet of the vagabond and the proletariat. Unlike Chekhov's calm, cultivated voice or Tolstoy's apostolic one, Gorky's voice is the roaring of a lion and the crash of thunder. The note praises Gorky's courage in finding the vagabond and outcast more sublime than society itself.

His Bosyak, the barefooted dreamer who possesses nothing and fears nothing, is presented as a symbolic over-man, proud in idleness and gay in misery. Readers are primed for a novel whose hero carries that rebellious, irreconcilable spirit of future man.
the-motor-maid:
Title pages only are present here for The Motor Maid by C. N. and A. M. Williamson, published in New York by the A. L. Burt Company, so the motoring story does not appear. Four illustrations in colour by F. M. Du Mond and F. Lowenheim are promised. A caption quotes the travellers racing along a clear road with the Etang shimmering blue before them.

Facing pages list other books by the Williamsons, ten in all. Lord Loveland Discovers America, Set in Silver, and The Lightning Conductor head the list. The Princess Passes, My Friend the Chauffeur, Lady Betty Across the Water, and The Car of Destiny show the pair's line in travel romance.
the-price-she-paid:
David Graham Phillips's novel The Price She Paid opens with a death and a verdict. Henry Gower is dead at sixty-one, and the narrator calls his whole life a fraud that was never suspected. Gower passed for a generous, warm-hearted man who could deny others nothing. In fact, the narrator says, he never once thought or acted except for his own comfort. His cheer and kindness were tools, since they kept those around him happy and ready to serve his wishes.

A few days after the death, the trick nearly comes out. His widow sits with her son Frank and daughter Mildred, planning the future. She laments that Henry never thought what would become of them. Frank notes that his father always made a big income yet saved nothing. Mother and daughter still cry that he was generous and the best father who ever lived.
the-ramblin-kid: Earl Wayland Bowman published his western in 1920. W. H. D. Koerner supplied the frontispiece. Eighteen chapters move from a night letter onward. A bluff is called, and questions of identity follow. An unused plate and a duel of endurance come next. Greedy sands threaten the riders. A dance and a ride lighten the middle. An amusement parlor and a grand parade lead toward sweepstakes. Only the title pages and contents list are present here. The kid's rambling itself does not appear.
the-romantic-adventures-of-a-milkmaid:
A tale set on a May morning in the eighteen forties opens in thick white fog. The fog hangs over the Valley of the Exe. The text was transcribed from the 1920 Macmillan edition of A Changed Man and Other Tales. The narrator relies on a land-surveyor for his particulars. He describes a scene heard rather than seen.

Lowing cattle and human voices rise through the fog. A dog barks, and a gate slams. Those sounds tell listeners what is happening below. Dairyman Tucker's under-milker is driving cows into the stalls. Tucker then sends the milkmaid Margery down the road. She must be back by skimming-time. She rises out of the fog in a bright pink cotton frock. A small woollen shawl completes her dress.
the-vision-splendid:
William MacLeod Raine opens The Vision Splendid with a passage from a dreamer's notebook on heredity and environment. We swim, it says, in cross currents of fate, guessing at life more than knowing it. Part one, A Rebel in the Making, then shows a lean, hatchet-faced boy trapped in school on a young spring day.

The boy stares past his state capitals toward a silvery river gleam through the firs. Locusts whirr, bluebirds sing, and nature's waking call drums in his heart. At recess he keeps perfect decorum, slips out the back way, and hides in tall ferns until the bell recalls his classmates. Then he runs to the river and watches trout hold motionless under the bank.
the-woman-who-did: Grant Allen's The Woman Who Did, dated 1895, opens with a dedication to his wife and a short preface. Allen recalls a friend doubting any woman would dare such a course. He answers that he knew a woman who did, and tells her story. A list of twenty-five chapters follows, without their text. The chapters themselves do not appear in the pages present here.
three-men-and-a-maid:
P. G. Wodehouse published his comic novel in 1921, opening in a furnished New York apartment rented by Mrs. Horace Hignett. Three clocks disagree wildly, yet Mrs. Hignett wakes at exactly eight, as always. She is the famous writer on theosophy, author of The Spreading Light.

Wodehouse explains her American lecture tour amid a 1921 swarm of British lecturers hunting easy money. Novelists, poets, scientists, and plain bores all crossed the Atlantic that year. Mrs. Hignett sailed early, itinerary booked, determined to get hers first. Readers get Wodehouse satire aimed at lecturers, spirituality, and business sense.
what-diantha-did:
Charlotte Perkins Gilman wrote What Diantha Did, a novel that opens at the Warden house in California. The house looks grand, with pillared porches, a cupola, and heavy flowering vines. Heavy mortgages weigh on it just the same. Mrs. Warden and her four daughters rest in comfort while her son fights the debts.

Mrs. Warden spends her days making bright wool afghans that few in California need. Her daughters sit with her among the blossoms and wool. The home runs on ease for most and strain for one. Gilman's heroine, Diantha, stands against this world of dependence. Work, pay, and women's freedom drive the tale.
what-katy-did: The pages here hold Susan Coolidge's dedication poem for What Katy Did, and the story itself does not appear. Coolidge recalls six children who once played together under green boughs. Summer games, snow fights, and quick made-up quarrels fill the verse. Their mother, she says, always kissed hurts well again. Now the children wear bonnets and tail coats and sit on committees. Small children crowd their knees and beg for tales of the old home. The poem sets a warm frame for Katy Carr's story.
what-timmy-did:
Mrs. Belloc Lowndes wrote What Timmy Did, copyrighted in 1922 by George H. Doran. A verse from the Psalms about peril from the dog heads the tale. Chapter one opens with a phone bell ringing in the shabby, sunlit hall of Old Place. The house sits in a Surrey parish named in Domesday Book.

John Tosswill finds the modern phone odd in such an old place. His wife Janet runs in from the garden, gloves off, to take the call. A tired voice says London wants her, and she protests that it must be a mistake. Lowndes builds unease from a small, wrong call. A quiet home and a hidden threat meet early.
what-two-children-did: The opening pages here offer the title page, contents, and the first lines of a verse for Charlotte E. Chittenden's What Two Children Did, with the story barely begun. Hurst printed the book in New York in 1903. The contents name Beth and her dolls, a wedding, and a secret. Later chapters promise Beth's birthday, a lost invitation, and a trip to a grandmother's. The first chapter starts as a short song about watching the world speed past a train window.
